content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
30	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
31	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
32	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
33	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
34	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
35	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
36	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
37	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
38	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
39	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
40	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
41	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
42	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
43	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
44	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
45	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
46	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
47	
48	## Requirements
49	
50	- Python 3.11 or newer
51	- no third-party runtime dependencies
52	
53	## Run the service
54	
55	```bash
56	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
57	```
58	
59	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
60	has bound the port.
61	
62	## HTTP API
63	
64	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
65	
66	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
67	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
68	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
69	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
70	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
71	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
72	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
73	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
74	
75	### Tenants and quotas
76	
77	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
78	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
79	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
80	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
81	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
82	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
83	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
84	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
85	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
86	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
87	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
88	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
89	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
90	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
91	
92	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
93	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
94	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status
95	queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
96	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
97	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
98	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
99	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
100	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
101	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
102	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
103	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
104	the usual `409 conflict`.
105	
106	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
107	hold:
108	
109	```http
110	PUT /quotas
111	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
112	X-Tenant-Id: acme
113	
114	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
115	```
116	
117	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
118	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
119	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
120	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
121	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
122	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
123	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
124	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
125	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
126	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
127	
128	```http
129	GET /quotas
130	X-Tenant-Id: acme
131	```
132	
133	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
134	when the tenant has declared none.
135	
136	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
137	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
138	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
139	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
140	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
141	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
142	
143	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
144	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
145	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
146	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
147	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
148	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
149	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
150	
151	### Usage metering and billing
152	
153	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
154	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
155	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
156	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
157	metered action types are:
158	
159	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
160	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
161	  definition;
162	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
163	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
164	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
165	  `schedule_triggered`;
166	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made. A
167	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
168	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
169	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails.
170	
171	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
172	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
173	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
174	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
175	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
176	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
177	
178	```http
179	GET /usage
180	X-Tenant-Id: acme
181	```
182	
183	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
184	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
185	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
186	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
187	
188	```http
189	GET /bill
190	X-Tenant-Id: acme
191	```
192	
193	Returns the per-type bill:
194	
195	```json
196	{"bill":{"items":[
197	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
198	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
199	],"total":2100}}
200	```
201	
202	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
203	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
204	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
205	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
206	
207	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
208	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
209	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
210	
211	### Operational metrics
212	
213	```http
214	GET /metrics
215	X-Tenant-Id: acme
216	```
217	
218	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
219	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
220	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
221	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
222	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
223	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
224	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
225	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
226	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
227	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
228	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
229	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
230	
231	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
232	timestamp ending in `Z`:
233	
234	```http
235	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
236	X-Tenant-Id: acme
237	```
238	
239	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
240	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
241	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
242	  counts every recorded fact;
243	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
244	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
245	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
246	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
247	  result.
248	
249	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
250	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
251	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
252	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
253	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
254	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
255	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
256	completion or termination event.
257	
258	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
259	
260	```http
261	GET /metrics/export
262	X-Tenant-Id: acme
263	```
264	
265	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
266	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
267	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
268	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
269	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
270	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
271	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
272	
273	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
274	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
275	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
276	ordered by ascending label value:
277	
278	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
279	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
280	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
281	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
282	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
283	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
284	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
285	  unlabeled scalar samples.
286	
287	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
288	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
289	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
290	ends with a single newline.
291	
292	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
293	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
294	failures, and schedule triggers:
295	
296	```json
297	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
298	```
299	
300	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
301	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
302	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
303	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
304	  ended for that reason.
305	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
306	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
307	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
308	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
309	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
310	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
311	  another attempt, per node identifier.
312	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
313	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
314	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
315	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
316	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
317	
318	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
319	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
320	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
321	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
322	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
323	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
324	
325	### Health
326	
327	```http
328	GET /health
329	```
330	
331	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
332	
333	### Create a workflow
334	
335	```http
336	POST /workflows
337	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
338	
339	{
340	  "id": "order-flow",
341	  "nodes": [
342	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
343	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
344	  ]
345	}
346	```
347	
348	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
349	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
350	
351	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
352	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
353	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
354	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
355	
356	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
357	
358	```json
359	{
360	  "id": "order-flow",
361	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
362	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
363	}
364	```
365	
366	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
367	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
368	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
369	
370	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
371	
372	```json
373	{
374	  "id": "nightly-orders",
375	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
376	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
377	}
378	```
379	
380	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
381	
382	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
383	
384	```json
385	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
386	```
387	
388	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
389	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
390	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
391	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
392	`false`.
393	
394	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
395	
396	```json
397	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
398	```
399	
400	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
401	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
402	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
403	dependencies of its successors.
404	
405	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
406	
407	```json
408	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
409	```
410	
411	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
412	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
413	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
414	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
415	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
416	`retries_exhausted`.
417	
418	A task may instead declare an approval point:
419	
420	```json
421	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
422	```
423	
424	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
425	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
426	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
427	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
428	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
429	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
430	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
431	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
432	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
433	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
434	move the task.
435	
436	### Submit an approval decision
437	
438	```http
439	POST /executions/run-1/decision
440	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
441	
442	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
443	```
444	
445	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
446	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
447	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
448	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
449	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
450	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
451	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
452	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
453	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
454	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
455	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
456	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
457	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
458	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
459	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
460	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
461	404.
462	
463	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
464	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
465	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
466	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
467	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
468	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
469	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
470	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
471	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
472	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
473	shape and event stream.
474	
475	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
476	segment:
477	
478	```json
479	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
480	```
481	
482	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
483	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
484	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
485	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
486	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
487	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
488	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
489	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
490	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
491	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
492	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
493	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
494	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
495	loop node instead).
496	
497	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
498	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
499	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
500	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
501	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
502	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
503	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
504	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
505	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
506	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
507	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
508	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
509	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
510	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
511	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
512	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
513	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
514	belong only to their iterations.
515	
516	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
517	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
518	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
519	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
520	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
521	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
522	exactly.
523	
524	### Workflow versions
525	
526	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
527	
528	```json
529	{
530	  "id": "order-flow",
531	  "version": "2026-09-25",
532	  "nodes": [
533	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
534	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
535	  ]
536	}
537	```
538	
539	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
540	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
541	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
542	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
543	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
544	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
545	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
546	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
547	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
548	
549	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
550	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
551	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
552	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
553	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
554	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
555	
556	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
557	current version at the moment it starts:
558	
559	```http
560	POST /executions
561	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
562	
563	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
564	```
565	
566	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
567	
568	```json
569	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
570	```
571	
572	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
573	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
574	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
575	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
576	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
577	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
578	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
579	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
580	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
581	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
582	conclusions never change.
583	
584	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
585	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
586	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
587	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
588	stream with no added field.
589	
590	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
591	
592	```http
593	GET /workflows/order-flow
594	```
595	
596	```json
597	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
598	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
599	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
600	]}
601	```
602	
603	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
604	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
605	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
606	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
607	resources as usual.
608	
609	### Migrate a running execution to another version
610	
611	```http
612	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
613	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
614	
615	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
616	```
617	
618	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
619	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
620	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
621	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
622	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
623	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
624	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
625	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
626	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
627	carries the target version.
628	
629	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
630	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
631	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
632	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
633	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
634	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
635	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
636	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
637	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
638	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
639	
640	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
641	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
642	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
643	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
644	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
645	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
646	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
647	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
648	content.
649	
650	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
651	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
652	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
653	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
654	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
655	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
656	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
657	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
658	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
659	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
660	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
661	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
662	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
663	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
664	
665	### Start an execution
666	
667	```http
668	POST /executions
669	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
670	
671	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
672	```
673	
674	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
675	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
676	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
677	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
678	
679	An execution may declare a timeout:
680	
681	```json
682	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
683	```
684	
685	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
686	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
687	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
688	a timeout never expire.
689	
690	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
691	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
692	
693	```json
694	{
695	  "id": "run-3",
696	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
697	  "input": {},
698	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
699	}
700	```
701	
702	### Inspect an execution
703	
704	```http
705	GET /executions/run-1
706	GET /executions/run-1/events
707	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
708	```
709	
710	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
711	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
712	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
713	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
714	
715	### Webhook notifications
716	
717	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
718	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
719	
720	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
721	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
722	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
723	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
724	  reason);
725	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
726	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
727	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
728	
729	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
730	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
731	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
732	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
733	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
734	
735	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
736	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
737	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
738	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
739	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
740	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
741	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
742	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
743	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
744	triggered it.
745	
746	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
747	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
748	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
749	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
750	results as before.
751	
752	### Inspect the delivery history
753	
754	```http
755	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
756	```
757	
758	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
759	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
760	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
761	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
762	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
763	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
764	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
765	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
766	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
767	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
768	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
769	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
770	
771	### Schedules
772	
773	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
774	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
775	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
776	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
777	
778	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
779	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
780	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
781	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
782	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
783	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
784	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
785	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
786	
787	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
788	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
789	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
790	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
791	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
792	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
793	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
794	created is exposed through the status query below.
795	
796	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
797	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
798	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
799	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
800	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
801	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
802	
803	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
804	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
805	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
806	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
807	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
808	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
809	
810	### Declare or replace a schedule
811	
812	```http
813	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
814	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
815	
816	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
817	```
818	
819	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
820	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
821	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
822	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
823	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
824	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
825	
826	### Inspect the schedule status
827	
828	```http
829	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
830	```
831	
832	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
833	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
834	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
835	
836	```json
837	{
838	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
839	  "paused": false,
840	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
841	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
842	}
843	```
844	
845	The fields are:
846	
847	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
848	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
849	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
850	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
851	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
852	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
853	  `null` until the first period fires;
854	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
855	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
856	
857	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
858	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
859	
860	### Pause and resume a schedule
861	
862	```http
863	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
864	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
865	
866	{}
867	```
868	
869	```http
870	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
871	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
872	
873	{}
874	```
875	
876	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
877	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
878	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
879	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
880	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
881	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
882	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
883	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
884	
885	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
886	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
887	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
888	
889	### Checkpoints
890	
891	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
892	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
893	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
894	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
895	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
896	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
897	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
898	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
899	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
900	duplicating any node output.
901	
902	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
903	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
904	same state shape and event stream as before.
905	
906	### Complete the next ready node
907	
908	```http
909	POST /executions/run-1/advance
910	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
911	
912	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
913	```
914	
915	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
916	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
917	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
918	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
919	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
920	the status becomes `completed`.
921	
922	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
923	
924	```http
925	POST /executions/run-1/advance
926	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
927	
928	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
929	```
930	
931	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
932	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
933	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
934	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
935	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
936	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
937	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
938	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
939	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
940	
941	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
942	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
943	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
944	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
945	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
946	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
947	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
948	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
949	the execution stream.
950	
951	### Cancel an execution
952	
953	```http
954	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
955	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
956	```
957	
958	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
959	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
960	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
961	
962	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
963	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
964	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
965	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
966	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
967	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
968	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
969	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
970	
971	### Claim a work item
972	
973	```http
974	POST /executions/run-1/claim
975	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
976	
977	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
978	```
979	
980	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
981	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
982	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
983	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
984	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
985	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
986	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
987	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
988	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
989	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
990	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
991	
992	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
993	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
994	
995	```http
996	POST /executions/run-1/advance
997	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
998	
999	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1000	```
1001	
1002	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
1003	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
1004	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
1005	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
1006	an execution without any claim.
1007	
1008	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
1009	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
1010	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
1011	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
1012	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
1013	
1014	### Renew a lease
1015	
1016	```http
1017	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
1018	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
1019	
1020	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1021	```
1022	
1023	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
1024	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
1025	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
1026	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
1027	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
1028	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
1029	
1030	### Release a work item
1031	
1032	```http
1033	POST /executions/run-1/release
1034	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
1035	
1036	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1037	```
1038	
1039	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
1040	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
1041	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
1042	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
1043	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
1044	`not_found`.
1045	
1046	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
1047	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
1048	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
1049	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
1050	restarts.
1051	
1052	### Recover from a checkpoint
1053	
1054	```http
1055	POST /executions/run-1/recover
1056	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
1057	
1058	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
1059	```
1060	
1061	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
1062	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
1063	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
1064	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
1065	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
1066	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
1067	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
1068	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
1069	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
1070	execution state and events.
1071	
1072	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
1073	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
1074	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
1075	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
1076	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
1077	stays consistent with the materialized state.
1078	
1079	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
1080	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
1081	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
1082	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
1083	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
1084	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
1085	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
1086	
1087	### Replay
1088	
1089	```http
1090	POST /executions/run-1/replay
1091	```
1092	
1093	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
1094	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
1095	and the rebuilt execution.
1096	
1097	## Errors
1098	
1099	Errors use this shape:
1100	
1101	```json
1102	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
1103	```
1104	
1105	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
1106	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
1107	declarations and the usage, bill, and metrics queries require a tenant, and
1108	quota limits are positive integers validated by the
1109	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
1110	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
1111	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
1112	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
1113	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1114	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1115	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1116	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1117	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1118	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1119	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1120	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1121	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1122	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1123	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1124	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1125	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1126	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1127	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1128	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
1129	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1130	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
1131	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1132	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1133	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1134	A decision by an approver who is
1135	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1136	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1137	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1138	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1139	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1140	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1141	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1142	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1143	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1144	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1145	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1146	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1147	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1148	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1149	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1150	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1151	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1152	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1153	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1154	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
1155	
1156	## Tests
1157	
1158	```bash
1159	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
1160	```
1161	
1162
